title: Heat up and cool down: comparing land and water

links.note: Verified 2026-10-26: chapter 41675 (textbook extraction 858, page 3) lists A1 with task card G4_WATER_EO_STC_1. No stored concept or learning outcome of this chapter mentions heating, cooling or breezes, so no concept is linked.

intro.purpose: Observe how different surfaces (soil, sand, grass and water) heat up and cool down at different speeds. Use thermometers to compare how their temperatures change under a lamp or in sunlight.

objectives.text: Compare how fast soil, sand, grass and water heat up and cool down.
Understand how sea and land breezes occur and why coastal areas have milder weather than inland regions.

materials.text: Soil, sand, grass and water, one for each tray
A lamp, or a sunny place

safety.text: Do this activity with your teacher.
A lamp gets hot. Do not touch the bulb, and keep water away from the lamp and its plug.
Wash your hands after touching soil, sand and grass.

duration.note: The task card has two waits of 15 minutes each (steps 4 and 7).

steps.text: Each group will be given 4 trays.
Fill each tray with soil, sand, grass, and water, respectively.
Check the initial temperature of all the materials.
Put the trays under a lamp or in sunlight for 15 minutes.
After heating, record the temperature of each surface.
Now, remove the trays from the heat and place them in the shade.
Wait for another 15 minutes and measure the new temperature of each tray.
Write your observations on the sheet
Discuss how these temperature changes help explain sea breezes and land breezes, and why places near the sea have milder weather.

blocks.label: Your observations
blocks.hint: Write what you saw when you compared the four trays.

reflection.prompt: Discuss how these temperature changes help explain sea breezes and land breezes, and why places near the sea have milder weather.

expected.heading: What the textbook says to notice
expected.text: Sand and soil heat up and cool down quickly, while grass and water change temperature more slowly. Compare this with your own numbers.
